background.definition: Mitral insufficiency, or MR, is a valvular disorder involving any of the following: the mitral leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles and left ventricular free wall, resulting in abnormal leakage of blood across the mitral valve (MV), ie, from the left ventricle to the left atrium.

list.listitem: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is a common valvular disorder, which increases with age and occurs in up to 10% of the general population.
MR affects about 5 in 10,000 people and is the second most common valvular disease behind aortic stenosis.
Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is present in approximately 4% of the normal healthy population.
MR may occur acutely or chronically due to disruption of different parts of the mitral valve apparatus (leaflets, annulus, chordae, papillary muscle or LV free wall).

Causes of acute MR include spontaneous chordal rupture in patients with myxomatous mitral valve disease or rupture of the papillary muscle occurs in patients who have an acute ST-segment–elevation myocardial infarction, usually associated with inferior wall myocardial infarction.
Causes of chronic MR can be divided into primary (degenerative ) and secondary (functional) causes.
Primary chronic MR: In developed countries, MVP is the most common cause of MR and in developing countries, rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of MR

Other primary causes include infective endocarditis, trauma, drug-induced MR (medications that can interact with serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine 2B) receptors on cardiac valves (eg, pergolide and cabergoline)), and congenital MR.

Secondary MR: An enlarged ventricle can predispose a patient to MR. These secondary causes are (in order of frequency) ischemic heart disease, non-ischemic left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Pathophysiology largely depends on the cause of MR as described above.

In general, MR involves a transition from an asymptomatic compensated stage to a symptomatic decompensated stage. The rate at which this transition occurs is variable and is also dependent on the process causing the MR.
Treatment of streptococcal infections is recommended to prevent rheumatic heart disease.

Antibiotic prophylaxis with dental, respiratory tract, and skin procedures is recommended only for patients with the following cardiac conditions: prosthetic cardiac valve, previous endocarditis, and complex congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect.

Antibiotic prophylaxis for some procedures (eg, endoscopy with or without biopsy, transesophageal echocardiography, bronchoscopy, vaginal or cesarean delivery) is no longer recommended, even for high-risk patients.

Recommended prophylaxis regimen administered 60 minutes before the procedure: amoxicillin 2 g for adults or 50 mg/kg for children. If allergic to penicillin, alternatives include cephalexin 2 g, clindamycin 600 mg, azithromycin 500 mg for adults or 15 mg/kg for children, and clarithromycin 500 mg for adults or 15 mg/kg for children.

Echocardiogram is the gold standard for establishing and diagnosing the severity of MR and is indicated in any patient suspected of having MR. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Murmur heard best in the upper right second intercostal space; harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur
Heard best along the lower left sternal border; difficult to distinguish on auscultation from MR

list.listitem: American Society of Echocardiography criteria for the diagnosis of severe MR: regurgitant orifice area greater than 0.40 cm2, regurgitant volume greater than 60 mL, regurgitant fraction greater than 50%, jet area greater than 40% of left atrial area, and vena contracta (jet width at regitant oriface) >0.7 cm. Severe MR should exist with left ventricular enlargement. Left atrial enlargement (LAE) may reflect duration and severity of MR.
Clinical manifestations of MR depend on its severity. Patients with mild and moderate MR are often asymptomatic, and patients with severe MR can be symptomatic or asymptomatic.
The most common symptoms in severe MR are exertional dyspnea and fatigue. MR can present with new-onset atrial fibrillation.

The classic murmur of MRis a holosystolic murmur heard best over the apex and radiating to the axilla, with a blowing and high-pitched quality. The murmur becomes louder with increased afterload (eg, squatting, handgrip) and softer with decreases in preload (standing, Valsalva). It is also louder in patients with increased LV volume (eg, heart failure, leg raising, lying down). The S1 is diminished secondary to inability of MV leaflets to close properly. If MR causes a dilated left ventricle, S3 may be present as well as lateral displacement of apical impulse.
MVP is characterized by middle to late systolic click. However, it is only 10% sensitive and had a positive predictive value of 17% (ie, only 17% of those with a click have MVP by ECHO).
ECG may show left atrial enlargement (LAE), left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), and ST-T segment abnormalities.
CXR may show cardiomegaly from LVH and LAE. Calcification of MV may also be seen.
Echocardiogram is the gold standard for establishing and diagnosing the severity of MR and is indicated in any patient suspected of having MR.
A transesophageal echocardiogram aids in the confirmation of mitral regurgitation severity, establishing the mechanism of disease, and in planning possible surgical treatments.

B-natriuretic peptide (BNP) is recommended only for patients with suspected or known heart failure. It has not been shown to have any diagnostic utility in grading the severity of MR. However, there is some evidence to suggest a correlation of elevated BNP levels with poor clinical outcome in patients with MR.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated that predicts the likelihood a patient will need pacing after valve surgery. It is based on the patient's age, type of surgery, preoperative ECG, and history of previous valve surgery.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation and management.
Vasodilators are not recommended for asymptomatic patients with chronic MR. A
Medical therapy is beneficial in acute symptomatic patients and is directed at decreasing afterload with vasodilators (ie, hydralazine and nitroprusside) as a bridge to surgery. B
Guidelines directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure (HF) is indicated in chronic MR with systolic dysfunction.

Indications for surgery are the following: acute MR with CHF or cardiogenic shock, class II/III/IV symptoms with EF >30% and LV end diastolic dimension >55 mm, asymptomatic with ejection fraction (EF) between 30% and 60% and end systolic dimension greater than or equal to 40 mm. In patients with chronic severe primary MR that are minimally symptomatic, surgery is recommended if the likelihood of repair (versus replacement) is high. A
Medical therapy is directed at increasing forward flow from the LV.
A beneficial effect is seen in acute vasodilator therapy with nitroprusside and hydralazine for symptomatic patients as a bridge for patients who are candidates for surgery.

For chronic severe primary MR patients with LV systolic dysfunction in whom surgery is not possible or must be delayed, standard regimen for systolic dysfunction, including beta-adrenergic blockade, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and possibly aldosterone antagonists should be considered.
Patient with chronic severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) should receive GDMT for HF and biventricular pacing as indicated.
For patients with MR and atrial fibrillation, calcium channel blockers, β blockers for rate control, and anticoagulation with warfarin should be used.

Patients who have had a mechanical heart valve replacement should undergo lifetime anticoagulation with warfarin. A Cochrane review found that adding a low dose of aspirin (100 mg/day) to oral anticoagulation reduces the risk of embolism or death, but increases the risk of major bleeding.

Following transcatheter mitral valve repair (edge to edge) results were better in a propensity score matched analysis for patients with EF < 50% who received guideline directed therapy consisting of beta-blockers, RAS inhibitors, and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
Urgent mitral valve surgery is recommended in symptomatic patients with acute severe primary MR.

In patients with severe chronic MR, surgery is indicated for patients with symptoms despite medical therapy, asymptomatic patients with abnormalities in LV size and LV dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and new-onset atrial fibrillation. ,

In asymptomatic patients with severe chronic MR, surgery is indicated for left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 30% to 60% and/or end systolic dimension greater than 40 mm, or if surgery is highly likely to result in repair versus mitral valve replacement.

In primary chronic MR, MV repair is preferred over MV replacement, because many studies have demonstrated improved LV function and survival in patients undergoing valve repair. This is better performed at an experienced surgical center. See .

Recent data shows that minimally invasive mitral valve repair via thoracoscopically-guided minithoracotomy achieves high-quality and durable valve repair at 1 year with similar postoperative complications, when cmpared to conventional sternotomy.

An RCT randomized 279 patients with grade 3 or 4 mitral regurgitation to either percutaneous repair or conventional surgery. After one year of follow-up, the composite efficacy endpoint of freedom from death, surgery, or persistent regurgitation was more likely in the open surgery group (73% vs 55%, p = 0.007, NNT = 5), primarily due to more patients requiring surgery to repair the valve in the percutaneous repair group. However, major adverse events were much less likely in the percutaneous repair group within the first 30 days after the intervention (15% vs 48%, p < 0.001, NNH = 3).

When MV replacement is indicated, guidelines recommend that a bioprosthetic valve should be used in patients who cannot or refuse to take warfarin and in patients older than 65 years. However, a recent large cohort study found significantly higher long-term mortality among patients receiving a biological mitral prosthesis compared to those receiving a mechanical prosthesis, especially among younger patients.

A meta-analysis described lower perioperative mortality but higher recurrence of mitral regurgitation in patients undergoing mitral valve repair versus replacement, but no long term outcome differences were detected.
Coronary angiography is generally recommended before MV surgery as bypass surgery may be recommended concurrently with MV surgery.

Percutaneous mitral valve repair (pMVR) with the Mitra-clip device for functional mitral regurgitation complicated by heart failure is associated with improved functional class and improved hemodynamics; this procedure is typically reserved for patients deemed high risk for surgery. Lower heart failure hospitalization and all-cause mortality was observed at 24 months when compared to medical therapy.

A systematic review with 14 randomized trials and 2593 patients concluded that the durability of mitral valve repair was inferior with pMVR with the MitraClip compared with surgery with regards to the durability of the valve repair but not with regards to mortality at 12 and 24 months. It was superior to medical therapy though.
A small non-randomized study (n=126) concluded that the results of mitral transcatheter edge to edge repair may be superior if following cardiac resynchronization therapy.

A study identified 401 patients with moderate tricuspid regurgitation or less than moderate TR plus annular dilitation who were undergoing mitral valve surgery. They were randomized to tricuspid annuloplasty or no tricuspid repair. Over 2 years of follow-up, patients undergoing the tricuspid repair had significantly less likelihood of progression (0.6% vs 6.1%) but there was no difference in mortality or cardiovascular events and a much greater likelihood of pacemaker implantation in the tricuspid repair group (14.1% vs 2.5%).

In a large nationally representative cohort of patients with failed/degenerated bioprosthetic mitral valves, valve-in-valve transcatheter mitral valve replacement appeared to confer a short-term advantage over surgical reperative mitral valve replacement (re-SMVR) in terms of morbidity, discharge home, and length of stay but yielded equivalent outcomes for mortality and readmission.
Patients who have undergone surgery should not participate in any sport that may cause body contact because of the possibility that the MV repair will be disrupted.
Primary valve failure occurs in 44% receiving a bioprosthetic valve versus 4% receiving a mechanical valve (older than 15 years). B
After 15 years, all-cause mortality was the same between mechanical and bioprosthesis valves (81% vs 79%). B
MVP is not associated with an increase stroke risk.
MVP is not associated with any adverse cardiovascular outcomes.
In a 15-year follow-up period, patients undergoing MV replacement showed primary valve failure in 44% of those receiving a bioprosthetic valve versus 4% of those receiving a mechanical valve.
After 15 years, all-cause mortality was the same between mechanical and bioprosthesis valves (81% and 79%, respectively).
Among patients with heart failure, transcathether edge-to-edge repair of moderate or severe secondary MR leads to lower 5 year heart failure hospitalization an all cause mortality.

Compared with GDMT alone, patients with HF and severe secondary mitral regurgitation who underwent percutaneous edge-to edge repair system had lower 2-year rates of fatal and nonfatal all-cause hospitalizations and HFH and spent more time alive and out of the hospital.
For chronic MR, serial monitoring with echocardiography is important in recognizing the transition from a compensated to decompensated state and the need for surgical intervention.
Patients with mild MR should be seen yearly for history and physical.
Patients with moderate MR should be seen yearly and have repeat echocardiograms at these visits.
Patients with severe MR should be seen every 6 to 12 months or sooner if symptoms occur.
No contact sports; these sports may dislodge the valve.
Emphasize importance of antibiotic prophylaxis if mitral valve replacement or repair has taken place, and if necessary anticoagulation.
